title: Search under heavy load
response: Display other users’ eligible items loaded from the remote database
explanation: SP1: Search latency is sensitive to dataset size, query selectivity, payload size and concurrent request load; SearchActivity.keywordSearch() currently reloads local data and scans item words. In the remote design, pagination, indexed server-side filtering and payload limits therefore strongly affect the original sub-second goal. Heavy-load compliance is unverified because no remote implementation or load measurements were supplied.

title: Create an account and store it externally
stimulus: Creates an account with username and email
response: Create account and open home page
measure: Time until account is stored externally
explanation: RK1: UserList.saveUsers() writes a local JSON file, so the delivered implementation does not establish a shared remote account visible to both clients. The proposed server/database path needs an atomic unique-username constraint, durable commit and confirmation only after success. Otherwise two clients can create conflicting identities or see a success page before the shared account exists.

title: Log in and load an account externally
response: Open the home page using the account
measure: Time until account is loaded externally
explanation: RK2: LoginActivity.login() obtains an existing user ID from the entered username without proof that the caller owns that identity, while accounts are loaded from local files. A remote version must load the authoritative account and establish a verified session before exposing its home page or allowing owner actions. Username-only identification and fast loading must not be mistaken for secure authentication.

title: Reject an item with an empty field
stimulus: Attempts item creation with a required field empty
response: Display an input error and do not create the item
measure: Time to validate input and show feedback
explanation: NR1: AddItemActivity.saveItem() invokes validateInput(), which sets a field error and returns before creating or saving an item when a required field is the empty string. This local, early rejection supports the exact empty-field scenario without waiting for remote storage. The timing target remains unmeasured, and this finding does not cover whitespace-only strings, malformed numbers or server-side validation.

title: Save a valid item from the web application
measure: Time for server save and confirmation
explanation: TP1: Waiting for a durable database commit before confirming a web save protects integrity and shared-client visibility but adds network and storage latency to the user response. Confirming optimistically can reduce perceived latency while risking a false success if persistence fails; the local save path already conditions navigation on a successful save result. The target design should favor truthful post-commit confirmation and meet the latency target through efficient queries rather than premature acknowledgement.

title: Push changes from external systems
stimulus: Changes data used by the applications
measure: Time to send committed changes to clients
explanation: RK3: Observable.notifyObservers() calls in-process observers and cannot push external database changes to separate phones or browsers. Neither the local code nor the earlier conceptual server diagrams define a cross-client event channel, ordering or reconnect recovery. A commit-triggered event path with versioned messages and resynchronization is needed to avoid indefinitely stale application views.

title: Two users modify the same data
stimulus: Submit changes to the same record
response: Finish the first request, push its update, and process the next only if consistent
measure: Time to send updates while preserving consistency
explanation: RK4: Local list/file replacement and a common server host do not establish serialization or atomic conflict detection across clients, so concurrent bids or item edits can overwrite each other. The application/database boundary needs per-item transactions or version checks that commit the first request, publish its version and reject or revalidate stale later requests. This preserves the supplied ordering requirement; locking and notification coordination also create a secondary throughput/latency tradeoff.
evidence: E5, E6, E7; proposed server path
